title: Jazz
subtitle: Improvisation, time, and an American sound born in New Orleans.

chapters.label: CHAPTER 01 · A BENT PITCH AND A NEW NAME
chapters.heading: Slang carried into print.
chapters.subheading: A slang term traced back to pep and energy.
chapters.body: The word jazz is believed to trace back to jasm, an 1860 slang term for pep or energy. In 1912, the Los Angeles Times recorded it when baseball pitcher Ben Henderson described a wobbling pitch. By 1915, the Chicago Daily Tribune placed the word in music. The American Dialect Society later named it the Word of the 20th Century.

chapters.label: CHAPTER 02 · NEVER PLAYED THE SAME WAY TWICE
chapters.heading: Notes that answer to the moment.
chapters.subheading: Improvisation and interaction over written scores.
chapters.body: Unlike classical performers who aim for fidelity to a written score, jazz performers interpret a tune individually, changing melodies, harmonies, and time signatures. Rooted in blues work songs and field hollers structured around call-and-response patterns, early Dixieland layered countermelodies. Later, modal forms abandoned chord progressions entirely to open space for unscripted soloists.

chapters.label: CHAPTER 03 · BETWEEN COMMERCE AND THE CLUB
chapters.heading: A restless art that refuses fixed forms.
chapters.subheading: From big band swing to the bare tempo of bebop.
chapters.body: During the swing era of the 1920s to 1940s, big bands worked from arrangements learned by ear or memorized. Bebop arrived in the 1940s with small groups, brief initial melodies, and open improvisation. Bruce Johnson noted a lasting tension between commercial entertainment and art, while figures like Duke Ellington simply called the evolving tradition music.
